detailed_rationale:
Aarti Pharmalabs (demerged out of Aarti Drugs in 2023) makes pharmaceutical intermediates and APIs -- a business where China-linked pricing competition and raw-material/forex swings routinely move margins more than volumes do. Q4 FY26 revenue was up 9% YoY to Rs 580 crore, and full-year FY26 revenue was roughly flat at Rs 1,798 crore versus Rs 1,771 crore in FY25. But profitability deteriorated: Q4 PAT fell to Rs 62 crore from Rs 89 crore, full-year PAT fell to Rs 176 crore from Rs 257 crore (down ~31%), and EBITDA margin contracted sharply to 23.13% from 31.21% a year earlier. The quant scorecard's own numbers show the same pattern -- revenue_cagr_3y actually negative (-2.2%) and revenue_growth_1y -14% on the specific trailing window it uses, alongside a genuinely healthy balance sheet: debt/equity of 0.35x and interest coverage of 7.85x, so this is a margin problem, not a solvency one.

The 'rising debt burden' language in sell-side commentary is worth a fundamentals check rather than a repeat: on the numbers available here, leverage is moderate and interest is comfortably covered, so debt is a watch-item rather than a red flag today. The core question is whether the FY26 margin compression (pricing pressure, likely with a forex/raw-material component) is cyclical or a step-down in the intermediates business's pricing power -- I do not have enough evidence from FY26 alone to call it purely cyclical, so I am not crediting a sharp margin-recovery scenario.

At a trailing PE near 35x, the market is still paying a reasonably full multiple for a business whose margins just fell by roughly 800bps YoY -- that combination, not any balance-sheet distress, is the reason for caution here.
recommendation_rationale: The quant score is Sell on both horizons (27.04 / 33.77) with no meaningful divergence toward Hold, and the fundamentals confirm a real margin-compression year rather than a data artifact. The balance sheet is genuinely fine (low leverage, strong interest cover), which is why this is not treated as a distress case, but a ~31% full-year profit decline alongside a still-full valuation is not a basis for overriding the quant Sell.
summary: Aarti Pharmalabs makes pharmaceutical intermediates and active ingredients. Revenue has held roughly steady over the past year, but profitability has weakened noticeably -- full-year profit is down about 31% and operating margins have contracted by roughly 800 basis points, largely on pricing pressure in the intermediates business. The balance sheet itself is healthy (comfortable debt levels, strong interest coverage), so this is a margin story rather than a solvency one, but the current valuation does not yet reflect that margin reset.
positive_para: The balance sheet is a genuine strength: debt/equity of roughly 0.35x and interest coverage near 8x give the company real flexibility, and India's pharma-intermediates and API exporters continue to benefit from a structural China-plus-one sourcing shift among global formulators. If pricing stabilizes, FY26's margin compression could prove to be a cyclical trough rather than a permanent reset.
negative_para: Margins fell sharply in FY26 -- EBITDA margin from 31.21% to 23.13% YoY in the March quarter -- and full-year profit is down roughly 31% despite flat-to-slightly-up revenue, which means the earnings quality of the top-line stability is weak. At a trailing PE near 35x, the market has not yet repriced for this margin reset, and the intermediates/API space remains exposed to Chinese competitor pricing that the company cannot fully control.
reverse_dcf_judgment: A ~35x trailing multiple on a business whose margins just contracted by ~800bps and whose profit fell ~31% YoY implies the market is pricing a fairly quick margin recovery back toward the ~31% EBITDA-margin level of a year ago. Nothing in the FY26 results demonstrates that recovery is underway yet -- Q4 margin was still contracting sequentially versus the trailing pattern -- so the multiple looks ahead of the evidence rather than behind it; this reads as fair-to-rich rather than cheap.
